name: Bulgare
lede: Bulgare is a muted purplish red that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates to 1892, measured about twelve units from the everyday name Raspberry.

sections.title: A name shaped like a nationality, unexplained
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places Bulgare on plate 5, position J7, and dates its first recorded use to 1892 [1]. *Bulgare* is the French word for Bulgarian, which suggests a tie to a textile or dye trade, but the dictionary gives no fuller account, so the connection is undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 lists do not carry the name separately, and the National Bureau of Standards circular cites only Maerz and Paul's entry [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[indian-lake]], [[pomegranate-purple]] and [[solferino]], at 3.8, 4.1 and 4.5 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 58 of 23,781 paintings, 0.24 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 21, rarer than 60 percent of the named colors we track [3]. The sample is too thin for a reliable single-painter or country figure, so none is claimed here [3].

The color peaks in the 1900s, 2.5 times the expected rate across 1,674 paintings from that decade, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent (71 percent of its 21 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match dates to about 1470, by Hans Memling, more than four centuries before the name's 1892 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
